Header:
Date: 2026-11-02 16:00 UTC
Duration: 58 mins
Attendees: Maya Chen (Redwood AE), Carlos Ruiz (Redwood SE), Ravi Patel (Tidewater Head of Platform), Alicia Gomez (Tidewater InfoSec), Tom Hayes (Tidewater Cloud)

Auto-generated Summary: medium quality transcript; some speaker labels uncertain.

00:00 - Maya Chen: Hey everyone, thanks for joining. Quick check — audio okay?
00:03 - Ravi Patel: Yep, good here.
00:07 - Alicia Gomez: good, thanks.
00:12 - Maya Chen: Great. Today we're aiming to run through a security posture deep dive for Tidewater's private deployment needs — specifically network isolation, ingress/egress, audit logging, and KMS. Carlos will cover the architecture patterns and I'll go through compliance artifacts.
00:30 - Carlos Ruiz: Hi all. I'll start with an overview of the two main deployment patterns we typically recommend: VPC-hosted private (control plane in Redwood, data plane in your VPC via private link) versus fully private on-prem package where control plane can be isolated. We'll call them "VPC Private" and "OnPrem Private" for this call.
00:50 - Tom Hayes: quick clarifying q, sorry — is the VPC Private option still keeping keys in our KMS or are keys held by Redwood?
00:58 - Maya Chen: Good call. For VPC Private we integrate with your KMS — AWS KMS, GCP KMS, or even Cloud HSM. Keys for encryption at rest are customer-managed, we do not hold your plaintext keys. In OnPrem we can use an HSM connector that your HSM team runs.
01:20 - Alicia Gomez: when you say "connect" is that via a dedicated tunnel or e.g., a forwarder that we host? We have constraints: no outbound connections from the secured subnet except to approved endpoints.
01:31 - Carlos Ruiz: Right. For HSM we typically support either an on-prem sidecar that talks to the HSM over the internal network, or a peered connection to your HSM cluster. If outbound is restricted, we deploy a small proxy within your network zone that the Redwood runtime calls over the VPC peering or private link — no egress to public internet required.
01:50 - Alicia Gomez: ok that helps — we need details on cipher suites and mutual TLS, plus the certificate rotation story.
01:58 - Maya Chen: We'll attach our cert matrix but essentially we use mTLS with mutual client certs for inter-service auth, and we recommend TLS 1.3. For rotation, Redwood supports automated cert rollover triggered by your PKI — we can run through the automation in the runbook.
02:15 - Ravi Patel: Another big one: data residency. Our legal team requires all inference logs and any request/response payloads to remain in EU West or on-prem. How does Redwood guarantee that?
02:25 - Carlos Ruiz: Good question. Two parts: first, routing — you can configure model routing policies that pin inference traffic to a specific region and block fallthrough to other regions. Second, storage — logs and artifacts for private deployments stay in the customer VPC or customer-managed storage; for VPC Private we store logs in the customer's S3/GCS bucket in your region, under your IAM roles. We also support IP allowlist so control plane calls are proxied through endpoints in your region.
02:49 - Alicia Gomez: are there any metadata fields that Redwood keeps outside the region? e.g., billing meta or usage counters for our account?
02:56 - Maya Chen: Billing meta can be optionally replicated to Redwood's hosted analytics; but for enterprise private we can mask or keep billing data in your account. We default to a 'data-minimal' mode for private customers where usage summaries are aggregated and anonymized, and raw logs never leave your environment unless you explicitly enable sending them.
03:17 - Tom Hayes: On network isolation: we need to understand the ingress pattern for model updates. We push model artifacts via secure transfer to the serving cluster; do you support only pull from our artifact repo or does Redwood push into our network?
03:30 - Carlos Ruiz: We'll outline both options. Preferred secure pattern: your artifact repo (artifact store) is set up with a short-lived credential that the serving nodes pull from via a private link. Alternatively, for on-prem, you can push artifacts into a local artifact cache we run on the cluster. Push requires opening an approved ingress path from your build system. Pull is often simpler from a security standpoint.
03:50 - Ravi Patel: About RBAC/SSO — Alicia manages identity for us. We need full SAML/SSO with SCIM provisioning, and fine-grained RBAC down to route/model level.
03:59 - Alicia Gomez: yes, scim for onboarding is non-negotiable. We want to ensure the person who can create a rollout is separated from the person who can change network policies.
04:10 - Maya Chen: Redwood supports SAML 2.0 and SCIM 2.0. RBAC has role templates and also supports custom role creation scoped to resources: models, routes, and audit access. Audit trails label actions with user identity from SSO and the originating IP.
04:27 - Carlos Ruiz: small caveat — in some on-prem installs where the control plane is fully air-gapped, SCIM provisioning will be via a connector or our IDP sync tool that you run internally. We can provide a signed connector that runs with least privileges to the internal IDP.
04:41 - Tom Hayes: for audit logs — retention, tamper evidence, and streaming to our SIEM is critical. We need WORM-style retention for some logs for 7 years. Can Redwood support that?
04:52 - Maya Chen: Our audit pipeline supports two delivery patterns: streaming to your SIEM (syslog or S3 event sink) and immutable backup snapshots. For WORM, we recommend using your own WORM-capable storage or a write-once bucket policy; Redwood can write logs to your customer-owned bucket with lifecycle rules defined by you. For tamper evidence we produce cryptographic hashes of log batches and can co-sign those with your key if desired.
05:16 - Alicia Gomez: Does that co-sign require HSM access?
05:19 - Carlos Ruiz: It can be done either by Redwood using a customer-wrapped key or by you signing the hash on your side; if you want full control we can send the hash to your HSM endpoint and request a signature.
05:30 - Ravi Patel: Competitor question — we had a POC previously with BigCloudAI and they required a separate VPC for inference. What's the difference with Redwood's approach?
05:40 - Maya Chen: Good note. Redwood's differentiator is that we offer both VPC Private where runtime lives in your VPC (native) and a fully on-prem option. We also emphasize smart routing and cache controls so you get consistent latency across modes. With BigCloudAI many customers saw complexity in aligning private networking for every model — with Redwood routing policies you can set rules by model or tag so not everything needs isolation.
06:05 - Tom Hayes: ok, let's talk about egress controls. Our security team will only allow egress to a fixed set of IPs and domains — how flexible is Redwood for egress firewalling?
06:16 - Carlos Ruiz: We support egress via VPC NAT/Gateway and you can apply granular egress rules. For VPC Private we provide a list of endpoints and cert-validated hostnames; for on-prem we provide a smaller set of management endpoints. Also we support configuring a telemetry proxy so that all outbound telemetry is funneled through your approved proxy.
06:36 - Alicia Gomez: and what about DNS exfiltration — do you do DNS-based telemetry or external lookups by default?
06:42 - Maya Chen: No external lookups by default. We avoid external DNS calls; any model artifact fetch is via your artifact store or explicit approved endpoints. We can run a hardened DNS resolver in-cluster if needed.
06:55 - Ravi Patel: Encryption at rest — we want AES-256 with customer-managed keys and quarterly rotation. Also key rotation must not break active KV cache for long-running sessions. Any guidance?
07:07 - Carlos Ruiz: We recommend rolling key rotation where new keys are used for new data and background re-encrypt jobs migrate older objects. For KV cache (we often call it KV cache or KV cache) we persist checkpoints encrypted with a key envelope. When rotating KMS keys we rotate the envelope keys first and keep the older master keys available for decryption of active sessions until migration completes; that's the usual pattern for no-downtime rotation.
07:35 - Alicia Gomez: you said "KV cash" earlier — well, we actually have long-lived sessions for some agents, so can't afford a cache invalidation that kills context.
07:43 - Carlos Ruiz: understood — we can provide a zero-downtime rotation plan in the runbook and a small test harness to validate for your longest-running session lengths.
07:54 - Tom Hayes: are there latency implications with HSM sign operations? We saw ~40ms per call in one vendor during inference ops which added up.
08:03 - Maya Chen: HSM signing on per-token path would be prohibitive. We don't do per-token HSM calls. Typical patterns: ephemeral session keys derived and cached in the runtime, HSM is used for key unwrap/wrap during session create or rotation. So per-inference latency isn't tied to HSM.
08:20 - Ravi Patel: Great. Now compliance mapping — Alicia is driving SOC 2 Type II this year and ISO 27001 next quarter. What evidence can Redwood supply?
08:31 - Maya Chen: We provide a standard evidence pack: SOC 2 audit report (redacted where needed), ISO control mappings, network diagrams, penetration test summaries, configuration templates for private deployments, and control narratives for encryption, RBAC, and audit logging. For customers in early stages we also provide a compliance checklist showing responsibilities (shared responsibility matrix).
08:51 - Alicia Gomez: Will you include control owners and sample config exports so our auditors can reproduce?
08:56 - Maya Chen: Yes — we can provide exportable config blobs and sample API calls showing RBAC changes with audit trails.
09:04 - Tom Hayes: on the topic of fallbacks — we run critical inference and want graceful degradation. If Dedicated capacity hits a limit do you offer fallback to smaller models in-region rather than failover to hosted region?
09:16 - Carlos Ruiz: Yes, routing policies can prioritize in-region Dedicated and then fall back to in-region hosted-compatible model variants. We avoid cross-region fallbacks if you configure strict residency. That said, fallback to a smaller model in same region is standard.
09:32 - Ravi Patel: We need to gauge the risk: if we allow fallback to hosted variants within the EU, is contractual data handling identical?
09:40 - Maya Chen: For hosted within EU region, data handling and encryption standards are the same; the difference is tenancy — hosted is multi-tenant logically isolated, Dedicated is tenant-specific hardware pools. We will mark that in the SLR and DPA.
09:54 - Alicia Gomez: ask: what about logging PII — we prefer redaction at ingress. Does Redwood support redaction or tokenization before logs are written?
10:03 - Carlos Ruiz: Yes, we have a pluggable pre-ingest hook where you can run a lambda or middleware that redacts or tokenizes sensitive fields. For private deployments that hook runs inside your network so no sensitive data leaves your environment.
10:20 - Ravi Patel: ok that's good. Next — penetration tests. Do you allow us to do a customer-led pen test or is it only third-party negotiated?
10:29 - Maya Chen: We support customer-led pen tests with an approval window; for on-prem it's typically easier. For hosted we have a safe testing window and rules. We'll share our pentest policy doc.
10:39 - Tom Hayes: can you share the network manifest templates?
10:42 - Maya Chen: yes, Carlos will upload example VPC templates — subnets, NACLs, SGs, egress rules, and private link endpoints — into the shared drive. (link: https://app.redwood.ai/security/templates)
10:55 - Alicia Gomez: what's the story on long-term archival encryption? If logs are moved to Glacier-equivalent, we still want SSE with our CMKs.
11:03 - Carlos Ruiz: You can set S3 bucket encryption to use your KMS CMK; Redwood will write to your bucket with the KMS header and permissions you configure. For long-term archives we support using your CMK and lifecycle to glacier, preserving key policy.
11:16 - Ravi Patel: I'd like to talk briefly about observability — the console will show token-level cost and latency. Are any console artifacts or traces stored by Redwood outside our region?
11:28 - Maya Chen: For private customers we can run the console in your VPC or run a restricted console in the Redwood control plane that only stores anonymized traces. We can provide audit hooks so raw traces stream to your ELK/Datadog.
11:42 - Tom Hayes: can we enable IP allowlisting for the console admin UI and SSO enforcement?
11:48 - Maya Chen: Yes, admin UI access can be restricted via IP allowlist and SSO is required for admin operations. We also support device posture checks via a CASB integration for extra controls.
11:59 - Alicia Gomez: I have one more: retention of customer key material if we terminate the contract. How do you ensure keys and data are destroyed?
12:07 - Carlos Ruiz: Deprovisioning options: we delete keys and zero out data according to a documented SLA, but if you're using your own KMS then keys remain with you and we delete references. We provide a cryptographic shred proof (audit) that shows deletion events.
12:21 - Ravi Patel: Ok, sounds promising. Any performance/throughput caveats for private VPC versus on-prem?
12:28 - Carlos Ruiz: There can be network latency differences — on-prem with local GPUs is lowest latency; VPC Private latency depends on your peering topology and cross-AZ traffic. We provide a benchmarking harness and will provision a small Dedicated trial to measure your 95th percentile.
12:47 - Maya Chen: quick recap of next steps — we'll send SOC2/ISO evidence pack and the network templates; Carlos will share runbook for KMS rotation and audit pipeline; Tom will share VPC diagram and egress allowlist; we'll schedule the diagram review early next week.
13:02 - Ravi Patel: sounds good. Alicia, anything else?
13:06 - Alicia Gomez: no, thanks — make sure the runbook includes the cert rotation steps and the SCIM connector config.
13:12 - Maya Chen: noted. Thanks all, we'll follow up with the artifacts and an invite for the diagram deep-dive.
13:20 - End of recording.
